title: Teja: low-density living on Subang Jaya's busiest stretch.
excerpt: Sean returns to a project he saw at launch, now completed, to check whether it lived up to the sales gallery. It did, and its rents have kept climbing.
takeaways: Just seven units per floor in each tower, with a carefully finished facility deck.
Prices have risen from about RM600,000 at launch to RM730,000 to RM780,000; furnished units rent for about RM4,000.
Highway and service-centre noise, a one-way access loop and more supply to come are the concerns.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: Teja is low density: seven units per floor in each of two towers, served by two passenger lifts and a service lift, with corner units reached by their own short corridor. The site's slope gives it a basement car park, unusual for a purely residential project, with a covered car-wash bay for residents.

The facility deck is covered and finished throughout: a lap pool, kids' pool and jacuzzi, barbecue areas with transparent roofs, a community garden, a reading room and a gym fitted with Technogym equipment. Units range from about 550 to 1,150 sq ft; Sean tours an owner's two-bedroom unit with two bathrooms and two parking bays, which has no balcony, given the road noise.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: It sits in the Subang Jaya City Centre master plan, beside the Toyota and Lexus centre and on the same road as Subang Parade and Empire, with a wide walkway towards the malls and the nearest rail stations, which are a walk away rather than linked. The Federal Highway entrance into Subang Jaya is next door, and it lies under a flight path.

sections.heading: Rent and returns
paragraphs: The project is sold out. Bare units now ask about RM730,000 to RM780,000, against about RM600,000 at launch, and fully furnished units rent for about RM3,900 to RM4,000 a month. Sean says rents along this stretch are reaching new highs every month, and the video notes that both of the owner's units were rented right after the visit.

pros: It delivers what the sales gallery promised, if not more: the common areas and the units meet or beat expectations, which is the developer's reputation, as the master plan fills in block by block.

A straightforward design built around residents rather than excitement: a proper pool and gym, every corner finished, a car-wash bay, and enough guardhouse, visitor parking and loading space for a low-density block, which should keep maintenance arguments down later.

Subang Jaya itself: rents on this stretch keep rising, with the Federal Highway, rail and malls close by, and the city is running out of land. It has schools from kindergarten to university and stays family-oriented and low-rise because of flight paths.
cons: Design niggles: a low ceiling at the entrance and kitchen, an exit away from the guardhouse, visitor parking taking up the drop-off instead of the basement, and a gym entrance with no canopy for the rain.

The micro site: workshop noise from the Toyota and Lexus centre in working hours, and Federal Highway traffic that gets louder on higher floors, though the windows block it well. The one-way road means a long loop if you forget something, and weekend double-parking around Empire adds to it.

Future supply: three to five more plots nearby are likely to become more high-rises, and Subang Jaya prices are now near RM1,000 psf. Being part of a master plan should protect early buyers' interests.

closing: A sold-out, well-executed low-density condo in one of the Klang Valley's most complete suburbs; just test the noise on your chosen floor.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this October 2026 episode and its video description. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three he doesn't, in his order, at the end of the video. An owner let Sean view the unit; prices and rents are as he quoted them.
